data.title: Žibrica – a Hallstatt guard hillfort above Štitáre
data.excerpt: The Žibrica hillfort, in older usage Zubrica, lies in the Zobor–Žibrica range above the village of Štitáre and has yielded evidence of occupation by the Lusatian culture and of the Hallstatt and La Tène periods as well as of the Middle Ages. It consists of two independent parts, an unfortified settlement on the slope and the hillfort around the summit, and its steep, waterless interior suggests that it served mainly as a lookout over the prehistoric route through the Nitra valley.

children.text: The Žibrica hillfort (or, in older usage, Zubrica), where occupation of the Lusatian culture and of the Hallstatt and La Tène periods as well as of the Middle Ages is documented, consists of two mutually independent parts (a settlement and the hillfort), linked only by a comfortable route which at one point was artificially constructed. The settlement lies on the southern slope of the cone-shaped hill of Žibrica and the hillfort extends around the highest spot height of this hill. The hillfort was first investigated by Š. Janšák at the end of the 1920s.

Life on Žibrica was concentrated towards the south-east for several reasons: it is the sunny side, sloping gently down to the valley plain of the Žitava and, most importantly, the nearest abundant spring of drinking water is today on the village green of Štitáre. The considerable distance of the hillfort from this spring made it necessary to establish a lower settlement, inhabited in times of peace, which has no defensive ramparts, structures or other security installations preserved to the present day (which, admittedly, does not rule out possible wooden enclosures that disappeared in time without a trace). The settlement, lying on a gently inclined, flat slope, likewise lacks any natural protection. Nevertheless, given that it lay on the easiest route of approach to the hillfort, it may have performed the function of a bailey, entirely separated from the stronghold proper. The only reliable evidence by which this hillfort can be identified is the large, indeed striking quantity of sherds found at the site in the 1930s.

The original ascent to the hillfort leads from Štitáre, from spring P (see the illustration by Janšák), towards the north-west along a mountain but distinct track. At a distance of 1 km above the village the track makes a small hairpin bend which skirts a deep hollow way with a footpath. The old route ran along this hollow way. At point b, on the 350 contour, the settlement begins and extends for a length of about 240 m as far as the fork c. At point d, on the 505 contour, the ascent to the hillfort turns from the north-west to the north-east. Since it runs along a steep slope, it had to be modified artificially; the inhabitants of the hillforts did this by cutting away the slope over a length of 300 m, which created the bank df (serving no defensive purpose) and, running parallel with it, a ditch along the bottom of which the old road, still used today, runs. At point h, at spot height 605, the road enters the hillfort. The settlement also extends over a flat ridge-like spur of the main Zobor–Žibrica range. The hillfort lies on the dome-topped summit of the conical hill of Žibrica.

The summit of Žibrica hill offers no remarkable natural security. All its sides are formed by a sloping hillside with a gradient of 30°, at most 45°. There is no steeper place here protected by a rocky precipice. Only the summit ridge, spot heights 622, 630 and 609, has narrow rock pinnacles, without any space for staying or settling. The summit of Žibrica is encircled by only a single rampart. Starting from the entrance to the hillfort at point h, at spot height 605, it runs north-east, at the same time climbing to spot height 611 (which is the highest point of the ramparts overall), from where it drops abruptly to spot height 580, continuing with slight undulations almost horizontally to the western side of the hillfort, to spot height 583. From there, proceeding south-west, it descends still further to the lowest point of the ramparts, spot height 570, from where in the same direction, and later in a great arc to the north-east, it returns to the gateway. The height of this circuit rampart towards the interior of the hillfort ranges from 0.5 to 2 m, reaching the latter dimension in only three or four places. Towards the outside the rampart merges with the natural gradient of the terrain, forming a steeper step in it, 6–8 m high. The rampart is clearly preserved thanks to the woodland that protected it; it measures 864 m in circumference and is built of material obtained on the spot (from the side towards the interior of the hillfort).

Only one entrance gateway can be identified with certainty, on the south-east. On the north-western side, near spot height 572, the rampart is also interrupted by an opening, but nothing can be asserted with certainty about its purpose or origin, since any other indications are lacking.

The area of the hillfort is c. 4.37 ha, yet it offers only poor shelter in comparison with other hillforts of this kind. A glance at Janšák’s contour plan and the relevant sections will convince us of this. They show that along the longitudinal axis of the hillfort runs a sharp, almost impassable ridge (section AB), with three steep elevations, beginning in the south-west with a rock and ending in the north-east with a rock, which is merely a great obstacle for the hillfort and no protection at all. The section across the hillfort tells us that the terrain here has a gradient of 50°, in places as much as 60°, which makes the erection of dwellings, or even mere encampment under the open sky, impossible. At such an angle of slope objects already roll downwards. Only a few smaller platforms along the north-eastern part of the ridge thus remained available for occupation, together with a 5–10 m wide strip running on the inner side parallel with the rampart, created by the cutting away of the material needed to build the fortification. Under such circumstances it was necessary to enlarge the surface suitable for habitation artificially. This was done by creating a whole system of larger and smaller terraces (t) scattered irregularly over the hillfort, among which terrace T deserves mention on account of its considerable size. These terraces were created by cutting away the slope. Terraces can also be identified on both sides of the road leading to the hillfort, in the section f g. The largest of them rests with its rear (western) side against the rocky ridge, which rises 14 m above its platform (spot height 609), and by its size and relative comfort appears to be the most important part of the hillfort, its core. This conjecture would also be supported by several shallow bowl-shaped pits on its platform, 150–200 m in diameter, which may be regarded as the site of some kind of dwelling. More such sites, here and there nestling against a rock or a slope, can be found on the hillfort, mainly on its eastern and south-eastern slopes.

The artificial adaptation of the surface to the needs of habitation was all the more necessary the less favourable the position. The unsuitability for habitation is increased by the fact that the ridge of Žibrica runs close to the south-eastern rampart and thus divides the hillfort into two unequal parts. The south-eastern part, facing the sun, is smaller and narrower; the western and north-western part, unfavourably placed with regard to the sun and exposed to the north wind, is much larger. This circumstance too justifies the conclusion that Žibrica is not a hillfort intended for permanent habitation. Its shortcomings in detail are offset by its considerable height above the surrounding plains and by its distance from suitable routes, which may have been the reason why stronger fortifications were not even built. The whole surface of the hillfort was indeed inhabited, but, given the unfavourable form of the terrain, more intensive life was concentrated on the terraces mentioned above. On Žibrica there is also, on the eastern slope, a funnel-shaped pit M, parallels to which are to be found, for example, on „Pohanská“. Its depth on the uphill side is 8 m, on the downhill side 2 m, and its diameter 6 m. At the lowest point of the hillfort, at spot height 570, immediately adjoining the rampart, there is also a large pit Z which, given its position, may have been a cistern for rainwater. Otherwise the water supply of the hillfort was provided solely by the spring mentioned above in the present-day village of Štitáre, whose use is also indicated by the settlement as a descending stage towards the indispensable water.

Surface finds of sherds were very abundant in the past; both hillforts were literally covered with them. Janšák found, for example, rims or necks of vessels, pieces of bases, sherds with strong elongated bosses attached close to the neck, and also fragments with decoration. The sherds are mostly assigned to the Hallstatt period. A La Tène and a Slavic sherd also occurred at hillfort II.

What then was the purpose of the hillfort on Žibrica, given that a person’s stay on it, especially in winter or at times of heavy rain and wind, was real suffering? Did the hillfort serve as a strongpoint in some military operations? But in that case the unfortified farming hamlet on the slope would have been the first to fall victim to an attack, and the warriors on the top of the hill, who depended on it for their supplies, would soon have succumbed as well! The hillfort therefore served mainly for guard duty. In performing this, people take turns, they are not bound to permanent residence and must therefore be content with very modest comfort. And since guards were posted on Žibrica, on whom and on what were they keeping watch? On the basis of archaeological finds from the Nitra valley it has been reliably proved that a prehistoric route from south to north ran along it, which we have become accustomed to label generally as the Amber Route. Along this route travelled armed expeditions of foreigners, which, in relation to the local population, brought with them the danger of conquest. Even the movement of such apparently peaceful caravans of merchants had to be watched very closely, and that, according to Janšák, was the task of the guard hamlet on Žibrica.

In 2000–2002 test trenching was carried out at the hillfort, which confirmed extensive occupation of the site in the Final Bronze Age, the Early Hallstatt period, the Middle and Late La Tène periods and in the Middle Ages. The excavation was carried out on one of the most extensive terraces in the north-eastern part of the hillfort, where intensive occupation was expected. Just below the surface they discovered an occupation layer with a disturbed settlement feature. Numerous graphite-surfaced sherds, daub, charcoal and animal bones were also found. In the areas investigated the earlier occupation had evidently been disturbed by later interventions. At the eastern edge of the terrace they identified a stone-and-earth bank which, measured from the level at which it was built, survived to a height of 1.10 m. It can be assumed that it was built to reinforce the edge of the terrace. Beneath the stone-and-earth bank lay an occupation layer of the Final Bronze Age. Bronze arrowheads of the Hallstatt period were also found at the hillfort.
Susanne Stegmann-Rajtár, who is carrying out survey work at the hillfort, states (1) that

as early as during the archaeological and geophysical survey in 1999 the most numerous find material from the Štitáre-Žibrica hillfort, Nitra district, was obtained from surface collection, and so test trenching was subsequently carried out here as well. Besides numerous fragments of Lusatian culture pottery, so-called Early Scythian bronze arrowheads of the Hallstatt period were also found at this site. Two of them came directly from the crown of the rampart in the southern part, one from the immediate vicinity of the inner face of the rampart in the western part. A larger number of them are said to come from this hillfort. During repeated surveys in 2000 and 2001, in addition to pottery of the Late Urnfield period, sherds of the Hallstatt period were also found, which indicated that occupation here persisted in this period as well. On the basis of stray finds it was possible to document occupation in the La Tène period, the Middle Ages and the modern period too.

According to Dr Rajtárová, the aim of the excavations at the Štitáre-Žibrica hillfort in 2002 and 2003 was to establish the overall time span of occupation and also to gain insights into the stratigraphy of the occupation layers. The excavation was carried out on one of the most extensive terraces in the north-eastern part of the inner enclosure of the hillfort, where intensive occupation could be expected. The presence of settlement features was also indicated by the results of the geophysical survey and of auger boreholes. From the investigated occupation layers I and II a large number of sherds was obtained, above all of the Final Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age; sherds of the La Tène period, the Middle Ages and the modern period occurred here only sporadically. The layers also contained a quantity of daub and animal bones as well as several pieces of charcoal. Beneath the stone-and-earth bank at the edge of the terrace several sherds were found which can provisionally be attributed to the Čaka culture.

Dr Rajtárová further states that although the sherd material comes only from the occupation layers, it provides important information on the cultural and chronological attribution of this site. The pottery is highly diagnostic, containing a large number of decorated sherds as well as fragments of various characteristic vessel types. The assemblage obtained has provided the first significant insights into the main focus of occupation at this hillfort of the Lusatian culture, which falls not only within the Final Bronze Age but also within the Early Hallstatt period. Occupation of the hillforts in the Tríbeč range in the Hallstatt period as well had long been assumed, but more diagnostic find material such as that from Žibrica had so far been lacking. Comparable vessel forms as well as decorative motifs are also known from nearby settlements of the same period situated on slopes or in the lowlands, for example at Štitáre-Panská hora or at Nová Ves nad Žitavou. Parallels to the graphite-surfaced amphorae with the characteristic decoration of multiple horizontal, vertical or arched grooves such as those from Žibrica also come from numerous Lusatian culture cemeteries of the Late and Final Urnfield periods, for example from Partizánske or from Andač. The forms and decoration of the Hallstatt-period pottery from Žibrica have parallels above all at sites of the north-eastern Hallstatt culture.
